channel.title: Signal Brief · Industry
channel.description: Signal Brief: the day in technology, in The Signal's own words. Every item is written from linked official sources and fact checked before publication.

item.title: IQM revenue up 51 percent as backlog passes €100 million
item.description: IQM Quantum Computers reported third quarter revenue of €8.86 million, up 50.7 percent on a year earlier, and an order backlog of €102.5 million after booking €42.2 million in new orders during the quarter. The Finnish company reaffirmed full year revenue guidance of €42 million to €47 million and closed its largest contract to date, a €33 million deal with the LUMI AI Factory. It also sold its first system in South America and a second system in Japan. Why it matters for tech: Order books are growing faster than revenue for a quantum hardware maker, which is the clearest signal yet that buyers are committing real money.

item.title: Protesters enter Microsoft data centre site in Amsterdam
item.description: About 100 protesters entered the construction site of a Microsoft data centre in Amsterdam, according to Reuters, in a protest against three 85 metre towers planned for the outskirts of the city. Amsterdam has banned new data centres until 2030, but the project dates to 2016 and proceeds as planned, with Microsoft as sole tenant. It is the latest in a week of actions against data centre building, after voters in the United States rejected data centre development in local ballots earlier in the week. Why it matters for tech: Data centre building is meeting organised local resistance in Europe as well as the US, and older approvals are letting projects proceed despite new bans.

item.title: Horizon Quantum plans to buy error correction specialist Entropica Labs for $27 million
item.description: Horizon Quantum signed a non-binding letter of intent to acquire Singapore based quantum software company Entropica Labs for about $27 million in Horizon Quantum Class A ordinary shares. Entropica Labs specialises in error correction and fault tolerance. The deal still needs due diligence, audits and definitive agreements. Why it matters for tech: Quantum software firms are consolidating around error correction, the capability every hardware maker needs before fault tolerant machines arrive.

item.title: Agility Robotics lists on Nasdaq as humanoid robots face scrutiny over scale
item.description: Agility Robotics, maker of the Digit humanoid robot, listed on the Nasdaq on November 5 through a merger with a special purpose acquisition company, becoming the first dedicated humanoid robot developer to trade publicly in the US. Digit robots already work at customer sites including GXO warehouses and a Schaeffler factory, and the next model, Digit 5, arrives in 2027 with 50 pound lifting and more than 20 hours of work per day. The company's filing shows $1.8 million of revenue in 2025 against a $140 million operating loss, and notes humanoid robots remain unproven at scale. Why it matters for tech: A public listing tests whether investors will fund humanoid robots before the market proves itself, and Agility's numbers show how early that bet still is.

item.title: CQMTEK raises more than $15 million to expand quantum measurement manufacturing
item.description: CQMTEK, the brand of Guoce Quantum Technology (Zhejiang) Co., Ltd, has raised more than 100 million yuan, about 15 million US dollars, the company said. The funding is for expanding manufacturing and commercial applications of its quantum precision measurement products. Why it matters for tech: Quantum sensing and measurement is drawing commercial funding alongside computing, with manufacturing scale as the goal.

item.title: IonQ completes $1.15 billion acquisition of security firm Elisity
item.description: IonQ has completed its acquisition of Elisity, a zero trust security company, in an all stock transaction. IonQ's own announcement says it issued 1.15 billion US dollars of consideration in common stock at closing, with up to 150 million dollars more payable if Elisity meets revenue milestones through January 2028, and that Elisity's technology complements its post quantum cryptography and quantum key distribution work. Why it matters for tech: A quantum computing company is adding an operating security business to its revenue base.

item.title: Quint Computing raises €9.1 million seed round for hardware level quantum error correction
item.description: Quint Computing has secured €9.1 million (10.2 million US dollars) in seed funding plus a €2.2 million European Innovation Council Pathfinder grant. The company says its architecture aims to reduce physical error correction overhead by up to 100 times, using continuous electrical control in superconducting circuits. Why it matters for tech: Error correction is where quantum hardware economics are decided, and investors are funding it at the hardware layer.

item.title: Apple home robot reported for 2027 at around $1,000
item.description: Ars Technica reports that Apple is preparing a roaming home robot for 2027, priced at about $1,000, with FaceTime and smart home controls among its functions. The device is reported to have backing from CEO John Ternus and a limited initial feature set. Why it matters for tech: It puts Apple into home robotics, a new product category for the company, at a four figure price point.
